nameStory: This tiny marine red alga is named after French naturalist Eudes Deslongchamps, who studied marine life in the 1800s. Like other members of the Banded Weeds genus (Ceramium), it gets its group name from the distinctive banded pattern that runs along its delicate, thread-like branches.
description: Ceramium deslongchampsii is a small, delicate red seaweed that grows in New England's coastal waters. This marine alga forms tiny, branching tufts that look almost like miniature red coral or fine embroidery thread. It's quite small and easily overlooked, typically forming small colonies attached to rocks, shells, or other seaweeds in shallow marine environments.

idTips.label: Banded branches
idTips.description: Look for distinctive dark and light bands running across the thread-like branches, creating a striped appearance visible under close inspection

idTips.label: Red coloration
idTips.description: Overall reddish or pinkish color, though may appear brownish when dried or stressed

idTips.label: Branching pattern
idTips.description: Repeatedly forked, delicate branches that feel soft and somewhat gelatinous when fresh

idTips.label: Small size
idTips.description: Tiny tufts that rarely exceed a few centimeters in height, forming small patches rather than large stands

idTips.label: Marine habitat
idTips.description: Always found in saltwater environments, never in freshwater streams or ponds

habitat: Found in shallow coastal waters of New England, typically attached to rocks, shells, or other seaweeds in the intertidal zone or just below low tide. Prefers areas with good water circulation and is most commonly spotted in tide pools or on rocky shores where it can anchor securely to hard surfaces.

seasonality.spring: Begin looking for new growth as water temperatures start to warm, with fresh red coloration appearing on established colonies.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season when colonies are most visible and vibrant, easiest to spot during low tides on calm days.
seasonality.fall: Still present but may begin to show signs of seasonal die-back, with some colonies appearing more brownish than red.
seasonality.winter: Reduced visibility as growth slows, though established colonies may persist in protected areas with milder water temperatures.

funFact: Despite being incredibly tiny, this little seaweed is actually more closely related to land plants than to animals, yet it lives its entire life underwater and gets all its nutrients directly from seawater rather than soil!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other small red seaweeds in tide pools, but the distinctive banded pattern on the branches sets it apart from smooth-branched species. Remember: "Banded like a barber pole" - the stripes are the key identifying feature.
contextualKnowledge: While called a "weed," marine algae like this are actually crucial foundation species in coastal ecosystems, providing food and shelter for countless small marine creatures. The term "red alga" refers to a major group of marine plants, not just their color.
compareHints: Compared to Red Hornweed (Ceramium virgatum), this species tends to be smaller and has more pronounced banding patterns. Both share the characteristic forked branching of Ceramium species, but the banding intensity and overall size help distinguish between them when found in the same habitat.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Red hornweed differs from its close relatives Ceramium deslongchampsii and Ceramium secundatum primarily in the details of its branching pattern and the specific arrangement of its segments, though these differences require close examination with magnification.
Compared to Red Hornweed (Ceramium virgatum), this species has more pronounced one-sided curving of its branch tips and tends to form denser, more compact tufts.
